performers: Royal Choral Society; Royal Albert Hall Orchestra; Malcolm Sargent, conductor
intro: Malcolm Sargent conducted the Royal Choral Society and Royal Albert Hall Orchestra in the “Hallelujah” chorus from Handel’s Messiah, HWV 56, at the Albert Hall on 2 April 1926. In the chorus, short exclamations of praise are followed by long held notes above fast-moving choral lines.

sections.label: A · Hallelujah in D major
sections.mNote: Strings play the opening rhythm; the four choral parts follow.

sections.label: B · “The kingdom of this world”
sections.mNote: The choir sings in even crotchets.

sections.label: C · “King of kings” on held A
sections.mNote: Sopranos and altos hold A above the other voices’ entries.

sections.label: D · Long notes in the tenors
sections.mNote: The tenors hold D beneath the quicker upper parts.

sections.label: Coda · Last Hallelujah
sections.mNote: The bass moves from G to D.

cues.title: Orchestral introduction and choral entry
cues.text: The strings play the rhythm of “Hallelujah” for three bars before the choir enters. All four voice parts then sing together, and the violins play short phrases in the rests between their repeated “Hallelujah”s.
cues.evidence: Handel, Messiah, Hallelujah, bars 1–11; Joshua Koo’s Mutopia full score, violin and choral parts. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: “The kingdom of this world”
cues.text: At “The kingdom of this world” the choir’s syllables slow to crotchets. The four parts move together while the bass descends beneath them.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 33–41, the setting of “The kingdom of this world”. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Entries on “And he shall reign”
cues.text: The basses begin “And he shall reign”, and the tenors, altos and sopranos follow in turn (bars 41–51). The theme leaps through the chord, then runs down by step.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 41–51; entries in bass, tenor, alto and soprano. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Royal Albert Hall concert, 1926
cues.text: This recording was made during a concert at the Royal Albert Hall on 2 April 1926. The Royal Choral Society sang with the hall’s orchestra, conducted by Malcolm Sargent.
cues.evidence: German National Library catalogue, Electrola EJ 39 (matrix E-CR.237-1A), identifies a recording made during the 2 April 1926 concert: https://d-nb.info/380148439. Sargent’s credit: the same performance was issued by HMV as D 1108 (matrix CR 237-1A). Internet Archive transfers of both sides of an HMV D 1108 pressing (George Blood, Leif Druedahl collection) credit the Royal Choral Society, Handel and Malcolm Sargent, “Recorded during the actual performance at the Royal Albert Hall, on April 2nd, 1926”: https://archive.org/details/78_hallelujah-chorus_royal-choral-society-handel-malcolm-sargent_gbia7012305b and https://archive.org/details/78_behold-the-lamb-of-god_royal-choral-society-handel-malcolm-sargent_gbia7012305a ; a discographic listing of the 1926 HMV Albert Hall sides gives “Hallelujah chorus”, HMV D 1108, CR 237-1A, conductor Malcolm Sargent: https://archive.org/details/04-royal-choral-society-raho-m-sargent-messiah-hmv-d-1108-1926-04-02-2_202207 ; Public Domain Project: https://pool.publicdomainproject.org/index.php?title=Electrola-ej39-04871 (all opened). The German National Library record names no conductor. The Royal Choral Society’s history has a succession of guest conductors between Frederick Bridge’s retirement in 1922 and Sargent’s appointment as permanent conductor in 1928, which fits a guest credit in 1926: https://www.royalchoralsociety.co.uk/history.htm (opened).

cues.title: “King of kings”, sopranos
cues.text: The sopranos take “King of kings” up to D, then rise through E and F♯ to G. Each note is held across the barline. Beneath the sustained soprano line, the lower voices repeat their short entries.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 57–68: sustained soprano proclamations on D, E, F♯ and G. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Electrola EJ 39, Good Friday 1926
cues.text: The Hallelujah is the second side of Electrola EJ 39. The first side carries “Behold the Lamb of God” from the same concert. 2 April 1926 was Good Friday, the day of the Royal Choral Society’s annual Messiah at the Albert Hall, a custom since 1876.
cues.evidence: German National Library catalogue: EJ 39 side 1, “Oh, seht das Gotteslamm”, https://d-nb.info/380148420, and side 2, the Hallelujah, https://d-nb.info/380148439, both recorded at the concert of 2 April 1926. Easter Sunday 1926 fell on 4 April. The Royal Choral Society’s history dates its annual Good Friday Messiah to 1876: https://www.royalchoralsociety.co.uk/history.htm

cues.title: Final “Hallelujah”, bars 92–94
cues.text: The quick repetitions stop, and a rest comes before the last “Hallelujah”. The choir now sings the word in long notes. The bass moves from G to D in a plagal cadence, and the choir holds the final chord under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 92–94: rest, final declaration, plagal cadence and fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: Composer who filled London theatres with Italian opera and later put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg had a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant, and Prince Ruspoli provided him with singers and instrumentalists to write for. In the Dixit Dominus of 1707, a setting of a Latin psalm, five choral parts move at speed, then some voices hold dissonant notes while the others move underneath. He wrote chamber cantatas for a single singer. In Corelli’s Rome he learned to write for violin alongside the voice.
